parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the median and quartiles for the weights of the female spotted hyenas.
(3)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
An outlier is defined as any value greater than c or any value less than d where $c = Q_3 + 1.5(Q_3-Q_1)$, $d = Q_1 - 1.5(Q_3-Q_1)$
(b) Showing your working clearly, identify any outliers for these data.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) Upper limit $= 59 + 1.5\times 14 = 80$ M1; Lower limit $= 45 - 1.5\times 14 = 24$ A1; Outlier 84 A1ft
Notes: M1 correct expression for either limit ft their values in (a); 1st A1 80 and 24; 2nd A1ft all outliers identified using their limits (must be stated in (b))

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The weights, to the nearest kilogram, of a sample of male spotted hyenas living in the Serengeti are summarised below.
(c) In the space provided in the grid above, draw a box and whisker plot to represent the weights of female spotted hyenas living in the Serengeti. Indicate clearly any outliers. (A copy of this grid is on page 9 if you need to redraw your box and whisker plot.)
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) [Box plot for females: box from $Q_1=45$ to $Q_3=59$ with median at $54$, lower whisker to 32, upper whisker to 80 with outlier marked at 84] B1; B1; B1
Notes: 1st B1 Box with whiskers drawn and $Q_2$ and quartiles ft from (a), condone 2 whiskers on RHS; 2nd B1 for only one lower whisker to 32 and no outliers; 3rd B1 for upper whisker to 80 or 77 and an outlier at 84. NB If there are whiskers at both 77 and 80 it is 3rd B0

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Compare the weights of male and female spotted hyenas living in the Serengeti.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) Any two from: The females are heavier than the males (on average). B1; The males have lower median than females. B1; The males have a smaller IQR than the females; The females have a greater range than males. [Comments just about skewness are B0]

questions.stem: The parking times, $t$ hours, for cars in a car park are summarised below. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Time }(t\text{ hours}) & \text{Frequency }(f) & \text{Time midpoint }(m)\\\hline 0 \leqslant t <1 & 10 & 0.5\\\hline 1 \leqslant t <2 & 18 & 1.5\\\hline 2 \leqslant t <4 & 15 & 3\\\hline 4 \leqslant t <6 & 12 & 5\\\hline 6 \leqslant t <12 & 5 & 9\\\hline\end{array}$ (You may use $\sum fm = 182$ and $\sum fm^2 = 883$) A histogram is drawn to represent these data. The bar representing the time $1 \leqslant t < 2$ has a width of $1.5\,\text{cm}$ and a height of $6\,\text{cm}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Calculate the width and the height of the bar representing the time $4 \leqslant t < 6$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) Width $=3\,\text{cm}$ B1; 1cm$^2$ represents 2 cars or 0.5cm$^2$ represents 1 car or their $h\times w=6$ or area $=6$ M1; Height $=\frac{6}{3}=2\,\text{cm}$ A1
Notes: B1 3 only; M1 may be implied by correct height; A1 correct height of 2(cm) and correct width of 3(cm)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median parking time for the cars in the car park.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) Median $=(2)+\frac{30-28}{15}\times 2$ or $(2)+\frac{30.5-28}{15}\times 2$ (o.e.) M1 $=2.266\ldots$ (or $2.33\ldots$) A1
Notes: M1 for any correct equation leading to correct fraction as part of $m=\ldots$ or $(m-[2])=\ldots$ Ignore incorrect end point and watch out for 'working down'; A1 awrt 2.27 allow exact fraction e.g. $\frac{34}{15}$ (allow awrt 2.33 [or $\frac{7}{3}$] if $n+1$ used)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Estimate the mean and the standard deviation of the parking time for the cars in the car park.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $[\bar{t}=]\frac{182}{60}=3.03\ldots$ B1; $[\sigma_t=]\sqrt{\frac{883}{60}-\bar{t}^2}=\sqrt{5.5155\ldots}$ M1 $=2.3485\ldots$ ($s=2.3683\ldots$) A1
Notes: B1 awrt 3.03 (allow exact fraction e.g. $\frac{91}{30}$); M1 A correct expression; A1 awrt 2.35 or 2.37

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Describe, giving a reason, the skewness of the data.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) Mean > median B1ft; Positive skew dB1
Notes: 1st B1 ft their mean and median (Allow 'larger frequencies at the start of table'). Do not allow comparison of quartiles unless correct values are seen (2sf comparisons) $Q_1=1.28$ or $\frac{23}{18}$ [$(n+1)=1.29$] $Q_3=4.33$ or $\frac{13}{3}$ [$(n+1)=4.42$] e.g. $2.1>0.99$ or $2.1>1.0$; 2nd dB1 dependent on previous B1 being awarded

parts.label: e
parts.text:
One of these cars is selected at random.
(e) Estimate the probability that this car is parked for more than 75 minutes.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) [75 mins = 1.25 hours] $(>75\text{ mins})=5+12+15+\frac{3}{4}\times 18=45.5$ or $(<75)=10+\frac{1}{4}\times 18$ or $28-\frac{3}{4}\times 18$ M1; $\mathrm{P}(T>1.25)=\frac{45.5}{60}$ or e.g. $1-\frac{14.5}{60}$ M1 $=0.7583\ldots$ awrt $0.758$ A1
Notes: 1st M1 for a correct expression for no. of cars longer than 75 mins or shorter than 75 mins; 2nd M1 $\frac{k}{60}$ where $44\leqslant k<46$; A1 awrt 0.758 allow $\frac{91}{120}$ (o.e.). NB Any use of the normal distribution is M0M0A0

questions.stem: Pieces of wood cladding are produced by a timber merchant. There are three types of fault, A, B and C, that can appear in each piece of wood cladding. The Venn diagram shows the probabilities of a piece of wood cladding having the various types of fault. A piece of wood cladding is chosen at random.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that the piece of wood cladding has more than one type of fault.
(1)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Fault types A and C occur independently.
(b) Find the probability that the piece of wood cladding has no faults.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\mathrm{P}(A)\times\mathrm{P}(C)=\mathrm{P}(A\cap C)$; $0.2\times(0.08+p)=0.05$ or $\mathrm{P}(C)=\frac{0.05}{0.10+0.05+0.01+0.04}$ or $\frac{0.05}{0.2}$ or $0.25$ M1; $p=0.17$ A1; $\mathrm{P}(\text{no faults})=1-(0.1+0.05+0.01+0.04+0.08+0.03+"0.17")$ or $1-["\mathrm{P}(C)"+0.10+0.05+0.08]$ M1; $q=\underline{0.52}$ A1
Ans only: They can get $q$ without finding $p$ so a correct answer to $q$ scores 4/4
Notes: 1st M1 using $\mathrm{P}(A)\times\mathrm{P}(C)=\mathrm{P}(A\cap C)$ allow one addition error in $\mathrm{P}(A)$ e.g. $\mathrm{P}(A)=0.11$; 1st A1 0.17 only; 2nd M1 $1-(0.10+0.05+0.01+0.04+0.08+0.03+"\text{their } 0.17")$ allow letter $p$ for 0.17, or $1-["\mathrm{P}(C)"+0.10+0.05+0.08]$ but need a value for $\mathrm{P}(C)$ [M0A0M1A0 possible]; 2nd A1 0.52 only (correct answer of 0.52 with no incorrect working is 4/4)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Given that the piece of wood cladding has fault A,
(c) find the probability that it also has fault B but not fault C.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $\mathrm{P}(\text{Fault } B \text{ but not fault } C\mid \text{Has fault } A)=\frac{0.05}{0.2}$ M1 $=0.25$ A1
Notes: M1 for attempt at $\mathrm{P}(B\cap C'\mid A)$ allow for $\frac{0.06}{0.2}$ or $\frac{0.05}{0.2}$, allow ft of their $\mathrm{P}(A)$ used in part (b); A1 0.25

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Two pieces of the wood cladding are selected at random.
(d) Find the probability that both have exactly 2 types of fault.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $\mathrm{P}(\text{exactly 2 defects})=0.12$ or $\frac{3}{25}$ B1; $\mathrm{P}(\text{both have 2 defects})=0.12^2$ M1 $=\underline{0.0144}$ or $\frac{9}{625}$ A1
Notes: B1 sight of 0.12 or $(0.05+0.03+0.04)$ only NB e.g. $0.12\times 2$ is B1M0A0; M1 $("0.12")^2$ where $0.1<"0.12"<0.2$, may see attempt at $(0.05+0.03+0.04)^2$ multiplied out but must have $\geqslant 4$ correct products; A1 0.0144 (o.e.) (correct answer only scores 3/3)

questions.stem: A machine makes bolts such that the length, $L\,\text{cm}$, of a bolt has distribution $L\sim \mathrm{N}(4.1, 0.125^2)$ A bolt is selected at random.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that the length of this bolt is more than $4.3\,\text{cm}$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\mathrm{P}(L>4.3)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z>\frac{4.3-4.1}{0.125}\right)$ M1 $=\mathrm{P}(Z>1.6)$ or $1-\mathrm{P}(Z<1.6)$ or $1-0.9452$ M1 $=0.0548$ A1
Notes: 1st M1 standardising, allow use of $0.125^2$; 2nd M1 $1-p$, $p>0.8$; A1 awrt 0.0548

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Show that $\mathrm{P}(3.9<L<4.3)$ is 0.890 correct to 3 decimal places.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\mathrm{P}(3.9<L<4.3)=\mathrm{P}(Z<1.6)-\mathrm{P}(Z<-1.6)$ or $2(\mathrm{P}(Z<1.6)-0.5)$ $=0.9452-0.0548$ or $2(0.9452-0.5)$ $=0.8904$ B1cso
Notes: B1cso sight of 0.8904 or better (calc: 0.8904014212\ldots) or a correct subtraction

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The machine makes 500 bolts. The cost to make each bolt is 5 pence. Only bolts with length between $3.9\,\text{cm}$ and $4.3\,\text{cm}$ can be used. These are sold for 9 pence each. All the bolts that cannot be used are recycled with a scrap value of 1 pence each.
(c) Calculate an estimate for the profit made on these 500 bolts.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) Number of unusable bolts $=(1-0.89)\times 500 [=55]$ M1oe; Value of bolts $="445"\times 9+"55"\times 1$ M1oe; profit $="445"\times 9+"55"\times 1-500\times 5$ M1oe $=1560$ pence A1
Alternative: $\mathrm{E}(\text{value of a bolt})=0.89\times 9+0.11\times 1$ M1oe; $\mathrm{E}(\text{profit per bolt})=0.89\times 9+0.11\times 1-5$ M1oe; Profit $="3.12"\times 500$ M1oe $=1560$ pence A1
Notes: 1st M1 $(1-"0.89")\times 500$ or $0.89\times 9+0.11\times 1$; 2nd M1 $"445"\times 9+"55"$ or $0.89\times 9+0.11\times 1-5$; 3rd M1 method for the profit or their $"3.12"\times 500$; A1 for awrt £15.60 or 1560 pence(p) [need units]. SC think 55 scrap loses 1p: 1st M1 for sight of 55, B1 for answer of awrt 1450p, score as M1M0M0A1

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Following adjustments to the machine, the length of a bolt, $B\,\text{cm}$, made by the machine is such that $B\sim\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ Given that $\mathrm{P}(B>4.198)=0.025$ and $\mathrm{P}(B<4.065)=0.242$
(d) find the value of $\mu$ and the value of $\sigma$
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $\frac{4.198-\mu}{\sigma}=1.96$ or $4.198-\mu=1.96\sigma$ oe M1A1; $\frac{4.065-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.7$ or $4.065-\mu=-0.7\sigma$ oe A1; $0.133=2.66\sigma$ M1; $\sigma=0.05$ (or awrt 0.0500) A1; $\mu=4.1$ (or awrt 4.10) A1
Notes: 1st M1 Forming either equation – must have $z$ value but allow $\pm z$ where $|z|>0.6$; 1st A1 correct equation $4.198-\mu=1.96\sigma$ - any form (or allow $z=$ awrt 1.960); 2nd A1 correct equation $4.065-\mu=-0.7\sigma$ - any form (or allow $z=$ awrt $-0.700$); 2nd M1 eliminating $\mu$ or $\sigma$ (method seen leading to equation in 1 variable); 3rd A1 0.05 (or awrt 0.0500); 4th A1 4.1 (or awrt 4.10 dep on 1st or 2nd A1). NB Candidate who assumes $\mu=4.1$ can get M1A0A0M1A0A1

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) State, giving a reason, whether the adjustments to the machine will result in a decrease or an increase in the profit made on 500 bolts.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) The mean the same but the st. dev. decreased or $\mathrm{P}(3.9<L<4.3)$ increased. B1ft; So the profit will increase dB1ft
NB Use of $+0.7$ in (c) $\to \mu=3.99, \sigma=0.106$, prob $\approx 0.80 \to$ profit down
Notes: 1st B1ft if $\mu=4.1$ then ft $\sigma$; if $\mu<3.9$ (allow any $\sigma$) otherwise need to see $\mathrm{P}(3.9<L<4.3)$ calc. If they have $\mu=4.1$ in part (d) then don't need to state 'mean the same' in part (e); 2nd dB1ft therefore profit will increase (o.e.) [$\sigma<0$ is B0B0]
